source_text:
Institutio sive Paraenesis ad monachos (recensio brevior)
ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΕΝ ΑΓΙΟΙΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΗΜΩΝ ΝΕΙΛΟΥ ΠΑΡΑΙΝΕΣΙΣ ΠΡΟΣ
ΜΟΝΑΧΟΥΣ.
79.1236 Ἀκρασίαν βρωμάτων περικόπτει νηστεία, ἀκολασίαν δὲ πορνείας
περιαιρεῖ ἐγκράτεια μετὰ προσευχῆς. Φιλαργυρίαν τὴν τῆς εἰδωλολατρίας μητέρα
συστέλλει ἀκτημοσύνη, μέριμναν δὲ σωματικὴν περικόπτει ἐλπὶς ἡ εἰς Θεόν.
Πλανώμενον νοῦν συστέλλει ἀνάγνωσις λογίων Θεοῦ, καὶ ἀγρυπνία μετὰ
προσευχῆς. Θυμοῦ δὲ καταδρομὴν, καταπραΰνει μακροθυμία, καὶ ψαλμῳδία.
Ἀκηδίαν καταστέλλει ὑπομονὴ, καὶ δάκρυα, λύπην δὲ κοσμικὴν κατασιγάζει τὸ πρὸς
τὰς ἡδονὰς μῖσος. Φιλοξενίαν κτᾶται ταπεινοφροσύνη, καὶ φιλαρχίας, καὶ ὑπεροχῆς
ἀποστροφὴ, ὑπερηφανίαν δὲ, τὸ ἀρχαῖον κακὸν, τὸ βδελυκτὸν ἐνώπιον Κυρίου, ᾗ
ἀνθίσταται καὶ ὁ Θεὸς, καταπαύει ταπεινοφροσύνη ἀμέτρητος, ἡ λέγουσα· «Ἐγὼ εἰμὶ
γῆ καὶ σποδός.» Καὶ πάλιν· «Ἐὰν μὴ Κύριος οἰκοδομήσῃ οἶκον, εἰς μάτην ἐκοπίασεν ὁ
οἰκοδομῶν,» καὶ φυλάττειν πειρώμενος. Ὡς οὐκ ἔστι τεθολωμένον ὕδωρ
καθαρεῦσαι μὴ μεῖναν ἀσάλευτον, οὕτως οὐκ ἔστι μοναχοῦ κατάστασιν ἐπιγνῶναι,
ἄνευ ἡσυχίας. Ὡς ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν ἀθλητὴν στεφανωθῆναι μὴ παλαίσαντα, οὕτως
οὐκ ἔστι γενέσθαι Χριστιανὸν ἄνευ ἀγώνων.
thought_title: Remedies for the passions and the need for stillness and struggle
orientation: Evagrius opens the work by listing each passion and its remedy, then states that a monk's state cannot be known without stillness and that one cannot become a Christian without struggles.
pass_a_gloss: Lack of self-control in foods fasting cuts around, and licentiousness of fornication self-control with prayer takes away. Love of money, the mother of idolatry, poverty draws in, and bodily care hope in God cuts around. A wandering mind reading of the oracles of God draws in, and vigil with prayer. And the rush of anger long-suffering soothes, and psalmody. Listlessness patience checks, and tears, and worldly grief the hatred toward pleasures silences. Hospitality humility acquires, and the turning away from love of rule and preeminence, and pride, the ancient evil, the abominable thing before the Lord, which also God opposes, humility without measure stops, the one saying: 'I am earth and ashes.' And again: 'Unless the Lord builds a house, in vain the builder labored,' and trying to keep it. As it is not possible for muddied water to become clear without having remained undisturbed, so it is not possible to know a monk's state without stillness. As it is impossible for an athlete to be crowned without having wrestled, so it is not possible to become a Christian without struggles.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the compound verb to preserve the physical metaphor of cutting away a passion.
Literal sense of the verb, conveying restraint by pulling together rather than cutting.
Literal meaning of causing to cease, applied to pride.
Literal rendering of the adjective to preserve the sense of boundless humility.
The participle continues the description of the humility that speaks the quoted words; 'it' refers to the house or the saying, keeping the Greek's compactness.
rejected: and the one who tries to keep it

choices.why: Literal rendering of the perfect passive participle, conveying water made turbid.

bible_refs.note: Ἐὰν μὴ Κύριος οἰκοδομήσῃ οἶκον, εἰς μάτην ἐκοπίασεν ὁ οἰκοδομῶν

pass_b_english: Fasting cuts away lack of self-control in food, and self-control with prayer takes away the licentiousness of fornication. Poverty restrains love of money, the mother of idolatry, and hope in God cuts away bodily worry. Reading the words of God restrains a wandering mind, as does keeping vigil with prayer. Patience and psalmody calm the assault of anger. Endurance and tears hold listlessness in check, and hatred of pleasures silences worldly grief. Humility gains hospitality, and turning away from love of power and preeminence, while humility without measure stops pride—that ancient evil, abominable in the sight of the Lord, which God himself opposes—the humility that says, “I am earth and ashes” (Genesis 18:27), and again, “Unless the Lord builds the house, the builder has labored in vain” (Psalm 127:1), and strives to guard it. Just as muddied water cannot become clear unless it stays still, so a monk cannot know his own state without stillness. Just as an athlete cannot be crowned without wrestling, so no one can become a Christian without struggles.

problems.quote: Poverty draws in love of money
problems.source_quote: Φιλαργυρίαν τὴν τῆς εἰδωλολατρίας μητέρα συστέλλει ἀκτημοσύνη
problems.why: "Draws in" means attracts; συστέλλει means contracts/restrains. Poverty restrains love of money, not attracts it.

problems.quote: Reading the words of God draws in a wandering mind
problems.source_quote: Πλανώμενον νοῦν συστέλλει ἀνάγνωσις λογίων Θεοῦ
problems.why: "Draws in" again mistranslates συστέλλει; reading restrains/contracts the wandering mind, not attracts it.
problems.fix: Reading the words of God restrains a wandering mind

problems.quote: Humility gains hospitality and turning away from love of power and preeminence
problems.source_quote: Φιλοξενίαν κτᾶται ταπεινοφροσύνη, καὶ φιλαρχίας, καὶ ὑπεροχῆς ἀποστροφή
problems.why: The English makes "turning away" a second object of "gains," but the Greek has φιλοξενίαν κτᾶται (gains hospitality) and then ἀποστροφή (turning away) as a separate noun, not governed by κτᾶται. The structure is: "Humility gains hospitality, and [there is] turning away from love of power and preeminence." The English conflates these.
problems.fix: Humility gains hospitality, and turning away from love of power and preeminence
problems.ruling: English makes ἀποστροφή a second object of κτᾶται ('gains'), but Greek lists it separately; conflates distinct clauses, misleading reader.

edits.old: Poverty draws in love of money
Reading the words of God draws in a wandering mind
edits.new: Reading the words of God restrains a wandering mind

edits.old: Humility gains hospitality and turning away from love of power and preeminence
edits.new: Humility gains hospitality, and turning away from love of power and preeminence

fixed: συστέλλει means restrains/contracts, not attracts; changed 'draws in' to 'restrains'.
συστέλλει means restrains/contracts, not attracts; changed 'draws in' to 'restrains'.
The Greek has φιλοξενίαν κτᾶται (gains hospitality) and ἀποστροφή as a separate noun; added comma to separate the clauses.

problems.why: The Greek participle πειρώμενος ('trying/attempting') has no subject in English; the humility is what speaks and tries to keep/guard, but 'tries to keep it' is dangling and loses the connection to humility's effort to guard the house.

fixed: The Greek participle πειρώμενος ('trying/attempting') has no subject in English; the humility is what speaks and tries to keep/guard, but 'tries to keep it' is dangling and loses the connection to humility's effort to guard the house. Changed to 'and strives to guard it' to connect the effort to humility.

last_rejected.quote: Endurance and tears hold listlessness in check
last_rejected.why: ὑπομονή means patience, not endurance; glossary mandates patience.
last_rejected.fix: Patience and tears hold listlessness in check
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπομονή covers both 'patience' and 'endurance'; within normal range, not glossary-breaking.

last_rejected.quote: the humility that says, "I am earth and ashes" (Genesis 18:27)
last_rejected.source_quote: ἡ λέγουσα· «Ἐγὼ εἰμὶ γῆ καὶ σποδός.»
last_rejected.why: The Greek ἡ λέγουσα refers back to ταπεινοφροσύνη (humility), but the English "the humility that says" makes it sound like a different humility, obscuring that this is the same humility already mentioned—humility itself speaks these words.
last_rejected.fix: the humility that says, "I am earth and ashes"—making clear this is the same humility's voice
last_rejected.ruling: English 'the humility that says' correctly renders ἡ λέγουσα referring to ταπεινοφροσύνη; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: The Greek participle πειρώμενος (trying/attempting) has no object "it"; the English "guard it" adds an object that misrepresents the syntax. The phrase likely goes with the preceding quotation, meaning "trying to keep/guard" [the house/humility].
last_rejected.ruling: Object 'it' is implied by context (Psalm's 'house' or humility); πειρώμενος φυλάττειν = 'striving to guard' is accurate.

last_rejected.quote: Humility gains hospitality, and turning away from love of power and preeminence
last_rejected.source_quote: Φιλοξενίαν κτᾶται ταπεινοφροσύνη, καὶ φιλαρχίας, καὶ ὑπεροχῆς ἀποστροφή
last_rejected.why: The Greek καὶ φιλαρχίας, καὶ ὑπεροχῆς ἀποστροφή is a separate noun phrase in apposition or continuation, meaning "and [it gains] turning away from love of power and preeminence" — but the English "and turning away" makes this sound like a participial phrase dependent on the subject, losing that humility also "gains/acquires" this turning away. The structure suggests humility acquires both hospitality AND turning away.
last_rejected.fix: Humility gains hospitality, and turning away from love of power and preeminence
last_rejected.ruling: English preserves that humility gains hospitality and turning away; καὶ connects both as acquired by ταπεινοφροσύνη without mistranslation.
